checks.claim: Stem: on most coasts the sea rises and falls twice a day
checks.note: NOAA: 'In general, most areas have two high tides and two low tides each day'; the Gulf of Mexico has one. 'Most coasts' is right.

checks.claim: Key: the pull of the Moon's gravity mainly causes the tides
checks.note: Grokipedia: tides caused primarily by the gravity of Earth, Moon and Sun plus Earth's rotation, the Moon strongest; NOAA tides02: the Moon is the dominant force.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the push of the wind on the sea
checks.note: NOAA lists wind as a local factor that changes water levels beyond the Sun and Moon's tides, not their cause. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: the warmth of the Sun; Earth's magnetism
checks.note: Tides are gravitational; neither heat nor magnetism drives them.

checks.claim: Context: the Moon heaps the water up, Earth turns each coast through the high water, the Sun adds a smaller share; storm winds pile water on a shore but do not make the regular tides
checks.note: NOAA: onshore winds pile water up, offshore winds move it away; these modify the tides. Grokipedia: wind setups of several metres in storms.

checks.claim: Key: on the side facing away from the Moon the ocean also rises into high water
checks.note: NASA: the oceans bulge 'on both the side closest to the Moon and the side farthest from the Moon'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: extra-low water / lying level / draining toward the Moon's side
checks.note: The far side has a second bulge (high water); the lows lie between the bulges. All three are wrong; 'single bulge' is the documented misconception.

checks.claim: Context: Moon pulls hardest on the near side, weakest on the far side, so as Earth is pulled toward the Moon the far-side water is left behind in a second bulge
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the weaker pull relative to the Earth's center results in a second bulge'; water 'left behind as the planet is accelerated toward the Moon'. This is the standard differential-gravity account, physically correct; NOAA's classroom version (inertia exceeds the weaker pull on the far side) says the same thing in other words. Acceptable as stated.

checks.claim: Context: Earth spins through both bulges, so most coasts get two high tides about every day, low tides between
checks.note: NASA: 'Most shorelines experience two high and low tides per day'; 'The low points are where low tides occur'. Equilibrium-bulge model is the grade-level simplification.

checks.claim: Key: on most coasts the next high tide comes about 12 hours 25 minutes after the last
checks.note: NOAA: 'High tides occur 12 hours and 25 minutes apart'; Grokipedia gives the main lunar tide (M2) a period of 12.42 h (12 h 25 min). Stem says 'On most coasts', which correctly excludes diurnal coasts.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: about 24 hours 50 minutes
checks.note: That is the high-to-high interval only on diurnal coasts (e.g. parts of the Gulf of Mexico); the stem's 'On most coasts' makes it wrong. Keep 'most' in the stem.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: about 6 h 12 min; about 3 h 6 min
checks.note: About six hours is high to low, not high to high; 3 h has no basis.

checks.claim: Context: most coasts get two highs and two lows every 24 h 50 min; low tide about halfway between, some six hours after each high
checks.note: NOAA: 'a lunar day is 24 hours and 50 minutes'; 'Most coastal areas, with some exceptions' get two highs and two lows. NOAA JetStream: high and low 'about six hours apart'.

checks.claim: Stem: high tide comes about 50 minutes later each day
checks.note: Grokipedia: successive high tides 'roughly 50 minutes later each day'; NASA: 'The extra time is ~50 mins'.

checks.claim: Key: because the Moon moves on along its path around Earth
checks.note: NOAA: the Moon revolves in the same direction Earth rotates, so 'it takes the Earth an extra 50 minutes to catch up to the moon'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Earth moves on along its path around the Sun
checks.note: Not the cause. (Earth's orbit actually trims a few minutes off the slip measured on clock time, since it lengthens the solar day; it does not cause it.) Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: the Sun moves around Earth; the sea rises more slowly each day
checks.note: The Sun does not orbit Earth; no daily slowing of the sea.

checks.claim: Context: Moon orbits the same way Earth spins; Earth needs about 50 minutes more to bring the harbour back under the Moon; Earth's trip around the Sun sets the length of the year, not the tides; the Sun does not travel around Earth
checks.note: All true as meant. Optional tightening: 'not the daily timing of the tides', since Earth's changing distance from the Sun does slightly change the size of solar tides over the year; as written the sentence is read in the context of timing and is fine.

checks.claim: Stem: the Sun has about 27 million times the Moon's mass
checks.note: NOAA: 'the sun is 27 million times more massive than the moon'. Check: 1.989e30 kg / 7.35e22 kg = about 27.1 million.

checks.claim: Stem: the Sun's tides are only about half as big as the Moon's
checks.note: NOAA: 'Solar tides are about half as large as lunar tides'; NASA: 'a little less than half'; Grokipedia: about 46%. 'About half' is fine.

checks.claim: Key: it is much farther away from Earth
checks.note: NOAA: tidal forces 'vary inversely as the cube of the distance'; the Sun is 390 times farther than the Moon. 27.1e6 / 389^3 = about 0.46.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: made of hot gas; pull blocked by Earth's air; heat keeps the sea down
checks.note: Gravity depends only on mass and distance; air does not block gravity; heat plays no part. All truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: Sun about 390 times farther than the Moon; tide = difference in pull across Earth, which fades faster with distance than the pull itself; composition irrelevant; Moon's pull passes through the same air
checks.note: NASA: Sun 'about 390 times farther away than the Moon' (149.6 million km / 384,400 km = 389). Inverse cube vs inverse square correct.

checks.claim: Stem: on some days the Sun, Moon and Earth lie in one straight line; record shows the tides around those days
checks.note: NOAA: at full or new moon the three are 'nearly in alignment'. 'One straight line' is the usual grade-level phrasing; 'around those days' covers the real lag of about a day before the biggest tides (Old Farmer's Almanac, almanac.com).

checks.claim: Key: higher high tides and lower low tides
checks.note: NOAA: 'the solar tide has an additive effect on the lunar tide, creating extra-high high tides, and very low, low tides'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: higher highs but same lows; lower highs and higher lows; twice as many tides
checks.note: Lows fall lower too; lower highs and higher lows describe neap tides; the number of tides does not change. All wrong.

checks.claim: Context: Sun's tide adds to the Moon's, bulges grow, water drawn from the lows; biggest range; called spring tides
checks.note: NOAA JetStream: spring tides when Sun, Moon and Earth line up, the largest range between high and low.

checks.claim: Stem: at first and third quarter, Sun and Moon at right angles as seen from Earth; tides rise and fall least
checks.note: NOAA: 'Seven days after a spring tide, the sun and moon are at right angles'; neap tides 'during the first and third quarter moon, when the moon appears half full'. NOAA JetStream: neap 'has the smallest difference between high and low tide'.

checks.claim: Key: neap tides
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Neap tides occur during the first and third quarter phases of the moon', with the smallest range.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: spring tides
checks.note: Spring tides come at new and full moon with the largest range. Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: ebb tides
checks.note: NOAA JetStream: the fall from high to low is the ebb tide; not a monthly phase. Wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: slack tides
checks.note: Slack tide/slack water is the short period of no tidal current; never a synonym for neap tide. Wrong.

checks.claim: Context: neap at the quarter moons, Moon half lit; Sun's pull works across the Moon's and partly cancels it; smallest range; ebb = falling tide; slack = brief still pause when the tide turns
checks.note: NOAA: 'the solar tide partially cancels out the lunar tide'. Slack as the pause when the tidal stream turns matches Wikipedia ('no movement either way in the tidal stream'); slack need not fall exactly at high or low water, but the context does not say it does.

checks.claim: Stem: spring tides bring the highest high tides and lowest low tides
checks.note: NOAA: extra-high high tides and very low low tides (of the lunar cycle).

checks.claim: Key: twice a month, all year round
checks.note: NOAA: 'Spring tides occur twice each lunar month all year long, without regard to the season.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices: twice a month in spring only; once a year in spring; once a month all year
checks.note: Grokipedia: twice each lunar month, name 'unrelated to the season of spring'. Once a month is wrong (new AND full moon). All wrong.

checks.claim: Context: at every new moon and every full moon, about twice a month in every season; the name comes from the water springing up, nothing to do with spring
checks.note: NOAA JetStream: name from the water 'springing or rising up'; NOAA: from the tide 'springing forth'. NOAA and NASA both place spring tides at full and new moon; the real peak often lags by about a day, which 'about twice a month' does not contradict. Optional: 'around every new moon and every full moon'.

checks.claim: Key: with no Moon, smaller tides would carry on
checks.note: EarthDate: tides 'would be only about a third of their current sizes, driven only by the gravity of the distant Sun'. Follows from NOAA: solar tides about half the lunar tides.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: tides stop for good; same tides; bigger tides
checks.note: The Sun raises its own tide, so they would not stop; with the larger lunar share gone they could not be the same or bigger. All wrong.

checks.claim: Context: the Sun raises tides of its own, about half as big as the Moon's; with no Moon the sea would still rise and fall, only by less
checks.note: NOAA: 'the sun's tide-generating force is about half that of the moon'. Correct.

unit_notes: All nine questions check out. Sources: Grokipedia Tide and Spring_tide, NOAA tides tutorial (02, 03, 05, 06, 07, 08), NOAA springtide fact page, NOAA JetStream, NASA Moon Tides, Wikipedia Slack water, EarthDate. The two-highs stems correctly say 'most coasts' (NOAA: 'most areas'; diurnal coasts such as the Gulf of Mexico excepted). The far-side bulge context uses the differential-pull account (Grokipedia, NASA), which is correct and compatible with NOAA's inertia wording. 'About half' for the Sun's tide matches NOAA (NASA says a little less than half; Grokipedia 46%). Two optional tightenings, not errors: 8846cf43e0 context 'not the tides' could read 'not the daily timing of the tides'; 5834d546f9 context 'at every new moon' could read 'around every new moon' (the biggest tides often lag by about a day).
